name: Peppermint (Mentha x piperita)
short: A 2025 letter is titled peppermint oil-associated hepatotoxicity. Oil by mouth: more adverse events than placebo in IBS trials, mostly mild, often heartburn. Review: bleeding risk on anticoagulants.
text: Most safety data concern peppermint oil taken by mouth in irritable bowel syndrome. In a meta-analysis of 10 randomised trials (1030 patients), adverse events were more frequent with peppermint oil than placebo (relative risk 1.57, 95% CI 1.04 to 2.37); an earlier meta-analysis of nine trials of enteric-coated capsules (726 patients) found these events mild and transient, with heartburn the most commonly reported, and an 8-week trial in 190 patients also found mild adverse events more common with peppermint oil. A 2025 letter exists with the title "Peppermint oil-associated hepatotoxicity"; it has no abstract, so what it reports, including any cases and their details, is not known from the cited sources. A review of supplements and bleeding listed peppermint among supplements associated with bleeding risk in people taking anticoagulants, while finding no evidence of bleeding without anticoagulants. In a laboratory cell study, peppermint oil inhibited the drug-metabolising enzyme CYP3A4 more potently than a low concentration of ketoconazole; this has not been shown in people in the cited sources. A case series described contact sensitivity to peppermint and/or menthol in patients with mouth symptoms such as burning mouth or recurrent ulcers.
